events.speaker: James
events.text: Right, let's lock down the Q3 roadmap. We've got three big items competing for bandwidth — the mobile app redesign, the API integrations, and the analytics dashboard. I think we lead with the mobile redesign. It's been on the list for two years and customers keep asking for it.

events.speaker: Nina
events.text: Engineering is aligned on mobile. We know the codebase well, the team is familiar with it. It's lower risk than the API work.

events.speaker: Raj
events.text: Agreed. Mobile has the most Jira tickets from customers. That's a clear signal.

events.speaker: Clara
events.text: From UX perspective, mobile is definitely overdue. I've got six months of research ready to go.

intervention.question: What's the brief if mobile is actually a symptom and the real problem is that customers can't integrate your product into their workflow at all?
intervention.context: Everyone just validated mobile by pointing at Jira tickets and research backlogs, but that's measuring pain, not opportunity. The API integrations got quietly deprioritized as 'higher risk' without anyone asking what becomes possible commercially if you solve connectivity first — that's the assumption worth stress-testing before Q3 gets locked.

events.speaker: James
events.text: Perfect, so mobile first. We can push API integrations to Q4 and the dashboard to next year.

events.speaker: Ben
events.text: Hold on — I need to flag something. Three of our top enterprise prospects specifically asked about the API integrations last week. Two of them said it's a blocker for signing.

intervention.question: What's the example everyone here is afraid to learn from — the product team that ignored their loudest existing users to close the deal that changed their trajectory?
intervention.context: There's a well-documented pattern in B2B SaaS where volume of support noise from the existing base consistently drowns out the revenue signal from prospects at the point of conversion — the companies that broke this pattern typically did so by treating sales-qualified blockers as a separate prioritization track from product debt. The structural precedent worth examining is how infrastructure and platform businesses have historically used 'lighthouse customer' integrations as the unlock that shifts the entire adoption curve, rather than treating API work as a backend chore.

events.speaker: James
events.text: Sales always says everything is urgent, Ben. We can't let individual deals drive the roadmap.

events.speaker: Ben
events.text: These aren't small deals. We're talking about £2M combined. But if the team thinks mobile is the priority...

events.speaker: Raj
events.text: The data supports mobile. It's not just one or two customers.

events.speaker: Nina
events.text: And we'd be context-switching the team if we pivot to APIs now. That's expensive.

events.speaker: Clara
events.text: Mobile research is already done. Starting APIs from scratch would set us back months.

events.speaker: James
events.text: So we're agreed — mobile first, APIs in Q4. Ben, you can tell prospects Q4 for the API work.

intervention.question: What's the brief if mobile isn't the product but the proof point that gets enterprise API deals signed in Q1 instead of Q4?
intervention.context: The team just locked in a sequencing decision based on sunk cost logic — research is done, context-switching is expensive — but nobody tested whether that sequence is the fastest path to the biggest revenue. If enterprise API deals are sitting in the pipeline right now, telling prospects Q4 might be the most expensive decision in this conversation.

events.speaker: Ben
events.text: I mean... okay. I just want it on record that we might lose those deals.

intervention.question: Who decided 'mobile first' was a sequencing law and not just the last thing that felt safe?
intervention.context: The team is treating sunk research cost and context-switching anxiety as strategic logic — they're not. The radical alternative nobody is saying out loud: run a two-week API spike in parallel right now, before Ben loses deals that will never come back in Q4.

events.speaker: James
events.text: Noted. Let's move on to resourcing.

intervention.question: Ben just told you he expects to lose deals and you logged it as a note — what's the actual number of pipeline at risk and why hasn't that stopped this conversation?
intervention.context: The team just converted a revenue warning into a procedural footnote to avoid reopening a decision that felt settled. If the client-facing consequence of this sequencing is quantifiable pipeline loss, that number needs to be on the table now — because 'noted' won't explain to leadership why Q3 deals walked.

events.speaker: Nina
events.text: I think we should also confirm we're not touching the analytics dashboard until next year. It's the most complex piece.

events.speaker: Raj
events.text: Agreed, dashboard can wait. Customers aren't screaming for it.

events.speaker: James
events.text: Good. Mobile, then APIs, then dashboard. That's the roadmap.

events.speaker: Ben
events.text: What about the performance issues we've been seeing? Three enterprise clients flagged slow load times last month.

intervention.question: What if we gave one enterprise client a janky performance fix duct-taped together in 24 hours and watched what happened?
intervention.context: We're about to lock in a roadmap while three paying clients are already complaining — that's not a planning problem, that's a fire drill in slow motion. Shipping a rough-and-ready perf patch to one willing client RIGHT NOW teaches us more about severity and priority than any backlog grooming session ever will.

events.speaker: James
events.text: That's an engineering maintenance thing, not a roadmap item.

intervention.question: Who got burned by treating infrastructure degradation as a maintenance footnote instead of a strategic priority, and what did it cost them?
intervention.context: The pattern of deferring performance work until it becomes a crisis is well-documented in platform businesses — where slow load times silently drive churn before they appear in any roadmap metric. The most instructive precedents come from SaaS companies that lost enterprise contracts not at renewal, but quietly during the contract period when power users stopped engaging, making this a revenue integrity issue disguised as a technical one.

events.speaker: Nina
events.text: We can handle that in sprints alongside the mobile work.

events.speaker: Ben
events.text: Okay. I just hope we're not building a beautiful new mobile app that runs slowly.

events.speaker: James
events.text: We'll handle it. Are we done?

intervention.question: If 'we'll handle it in sprints' was a credible plan, why did Ben need to say 'I hope' instead of 'I know'?
intervention.context: No one in this exchange committed to anything measurable — James closed the conversation with authority while the underlying performance risk remained completely unresolved. The team learns now whether there is an actual plan or just a social agreement to stop talking about it, before the client watches their beautiful new mobile app crawl.

events.speaker: Raj
events.text: I think so.

events.speaker: Clara
events.text: Yes.

events.speaker: Ben
events.text: Sure.
